title: Quant, Lesson 2: Samples, standard errors and confidence intervals - how precise is your number really
subtitle: Why every estimate has to carry an interval, and why three weeks of data is usually nowhere near enough
whyItMatters: Every number on an operations dashboard is an estimate drawn from a sample: average latency, error rate, conversion rate, the improvement from a release. If you do not know the standard error of that estimate, you will make decisions on noise and believe you are acting on signal.
openingQuestion: How fast does the standard error of the sample mean fall as the sample grows?
openingOptions: Inversely proportional to the sample size n
Inversely proportional to the square root of n
Inversely proportional to the square of the sample size n
It does not depend on the sample size at all
explanation: The standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n. The consequence is intensely practical and fairly brutal: to halve your error you need four times the data. That is why judging a product change on a few weeks of aggregate data is close to hopeless - the confidence interval around the improvement is wide enough to contain both a real effect and random fluctuation.

diagram.label: Confidence interval - the plausible range of the truth

realWorldExample.company: Judging a change on weekly data
realWorldExample.description: A UI change lifts the order completion rate above the control group by an average of 2 percentage points a week, but that gap fluctuates from week to week with a standard deviation of 6 points. After three weeks the standard error of the estimate is 6 divided by the square root of 3, roughly 3.5 points. The 95% confidence interval therefore runs from about −5 to +9 points. Put another way, three weeks of data cannot tell a good change apart from a lucky streak. It would take roughly 36 weeks for a 2-point gap to reach conventional statistical significance.

quiz.question: What does the central limit theorem actually say?
options: Every operational metric series is normally distributed if it runs long enough
Each individual latency measurement drifts towards the mean if you measure long enough
The mean of a large enough sample is approximately normal
The larger the sample, the smaller the variance of the parent population
quiz.explanation: This is why inferential statistics still works on operational data with fat tails, such as latency. But note the scope carefully: the theorem applies to the sample mean, not to individual observations - so it does nothing to rescue tail metrics like p99. It says nothing about the shape of the underlying series itself, which can stay violently non-normal forever. It makes no claim that individual measurements drift towards the mean. And the variance of the parent population is a fixed property of the process; collecting more data measures it more precisely rather than shrinking it.

quiz.question: What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean?
options: There is exactly a 95% probability the true parameter lies in this interval
The estimate is 95% accurate relative to the true value of the parameter
Exactly 95% of the observations in the sample fall inside this interval
Repeat the procedure many times and 95% of the intervals cover the truth
quiz.explanation: This is a subtle distinction but an important one: the true parameter is a fixed number, and it is the interval that is random, because it depends on the sample you happened to draw. The first wording is the Bayesian reading, which requires an extra assumption about a prior distribution. The second confuses a coverage probability with an accuracy percentage, which is a different quantity entirely. And the third describes a prediction interval for the data points, not an interval for the parameter - those two are usually very different widths.

quiz.question: How much data do you need to halve the standard error?
options: Twice as much, since the standard error is inversely proportional to n
Eight times as much, since the error falls with the cube root of n
Four times as much, since it falls with the square root of n
It cannot be reduced, since the standard error does not depend on n
quiz.explanation: Because the standard error is inversely proportional to the square root of n. This is a hard constraint, and it is why experiments on noisy metrics so rarely deliver the strong conclusions people want from them. Proportionality to n itself would be far kinder and is simply not what the algebra gives. The cube root belongs to no part of this formula. And the standard error clearly does depend on sample size - it is the whole reason more data is worth collecting at all.

quiz.question: Does measuring more often, from once a day to once a minute, give a more precise estimate of a metric's average growth rate?
options: Yes, the observation count rises more than a thousandfold against daily data
No - precision depends on the length of the window, not the frequency
Yes, and the standard error falls linearly with the number of observations
No, because per-minute data carries only noise and no information at all
quiz.explanation: This is a surprising result: sampling more finely improves your estimate of variability but does almost nothing for your estimate of the average trend. When you cut the period shorter, the average gain per period shrinks faster than the noise per period, and summed over the whole window the signal-to-noise ratio is unchanged. Counting observations is therefore misleading here. The standard error never falls linearly in the number of observations in any case. And per-minute data is genuinely informative - it is the workhorse for measuring variability - just not for the trend. The only way to pin down the average growth rate is to observe for more weeks.

quiz.question: Why are three weeks of data almost never enough to conclude that a change really improved a metric?
options: Because the team may have shipped other features during that window
Because three weeks has not spanned a full seasonal cycle of the product
Because the standard error is so large that a real effect and luck cannot be separated
Because the metric over the last three weeks was affected by a promotion
quiz.explanation: At the fluctuation typical of weekly aggregate metrics, it takes dozens of weeks of data to separate an improvement of a few percentage points from random noise. Concurrent releases and seasonality are real concerns, but they are second-order: even a change tested with nothing else shipping and across a full season would still fail the test on three weeks. A promotion shifts the level of the metric without widening or narrowing the interval around the gap. This is one of the most uncomfortable results of statistics applied to products - and the most widely ignored.

keyTakeaways: Standard error = standard deviation / square root of n; twice the precision costs four times the data
Every estimate must carry a confidence interval, or it is just a number with no context
Three weeks of aggregate data is not enough to conclude that a small change really works
Measuring more often improves estimates of variability but barely improves estimates of the average trend

practicePrompt.question: A change shows an average improvement of 4 points a week with a standard deviation of 20 points, over 10 weeks of data. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The change definitely works because the mean is positive
The standard error of 6.3 points is larger than the 4 points observed
Measuring every hour would be enough data to settle the question
The change fails: its deviation is too high
practicePrompt.explanation: The t-ratio is roughly 4 divided by 6.3, about 0.63 - a long way from statistical significance. This is exactly the position many product experiment reports are in: a handsome average, presented as evidence, that never actually clears the noise floor.

summary.keyIdea: An estimate without a standard error is not yet information
summary.formula: SE = s / √n; 95% confidence interval ≈ estimate ± 1.96 × SE
summary.commonMistake: Concluding a change works on a few weeks of data, where the noise is many times larger than the signal
summary.action: For any improvement figure you read, work out the standard error quickly before you believe it.

application.title: The professional reflex
application.message: When somebody hands you a number - latency down 12%, conversion up 3%, correlation of 0.4 - the first question is always the same: computed over how many observations, and with what standard error. If the person presenting it cannot answer, the number is not yet fit to decide anything.
application.secondary: A rough rule: with a standard deviation of 6 points a week, it takes about 36 weeks of data for a 2-point improvement to reach conventional statistical significance.

sections.text: With a running system you never observe the truth. You have a sample - a few hundred observations drawn from a process that is still running and still changing. The whole of inferential statistics exists to answer one question: given this sample, how confident am I entitled to be?

sections.title: The standard error of the mean
sections.label: A measure of how uncertain the estimate itself is

variables.name: Number of observations
variables.description: When estimating an average trend, n is really the number of independent periods (weeks), not the number of measurements

example.title: Why the square root matters so much
example.result: Four times the data for twice the precision
example.explanation: This rule explains why small changes are so hard to prove with data: the cost of extra confidence rises with the square, while the product and its users keep changing character over the very period you are measuring.

sections.text: The paradox of sampling more finely

Intuition says measuring every minute beats measuring every day because there are more observations. That holds for variability and fails for the average trend. The reason: as you cut the period shorter, the average gain per period shrinks faster than the noise per period, and summed over the whole window the signal-to-noise ratio is unchanged. The only way to become more certain about a metric's average growth rate is to observe over more weeks.

sections.label: What this means for judging releases
sections.text: If three weeks of data cannot separate a real effect from luck, then keeping or removing a feature on the strength of a three-week chart is acting on noise. This is one of the most common mistakes, and one of the most ignored, when product teams read the dashboard after each release.

sections.title: Eight weeks of data: what the confidence interval says
sections.task: Below is the average latency increase (%) for eight consecutive weeks after a release. Each week is an independent observation. Print the mean, the standard error SE = s / sqrt(n), the approximate 95% confidence interval (mean ± 1.96 SE), and a conclusion on whether the interval rules out 0. The starter computes SE as s divided by n.
hints: The formula in the lesson is s divided by the square root of n, not divided by n.
With only eight observations the true interval is a little wider than 1.96 SE. If this interval already contains 0, the conclusion can only get weaker.
sections.starter:
import math, statistics
tang_truong = [2.1, -0.9, 1.8, 0.9, -1.2, 2.5, 0.3, 1.0]
n = len(tang_truong)
tb = statistics.mean(tang_truong)
s = statistics.stdev(tang_truong)
se = s / n
thap, cao = tb - 1.96 * se, tb + 1.96 * se
print("Mean:", round(tb, 2))
print("Standard error:", round(se, 2))
print("Confidence interval:", round(thap, 2), "to", round(cao, 2))
print("Conclusion:", "different from 0" if thap > 0 or cao < 0 else "not enough to say it differs from 0")
sections.solution:
import math, statistics
tang_truong = [2.1, -0.9, 1.8, 0.9, -1.2, 2.5, 0.3, 1.0]
n = len(tang_truong)
tb = statistics.mean(tang_truong)
s = statistics.stdev(tang_truong)
se = s / math.sqrt(n)
thap, cao = tb - 1.96 * se, tb + 1.96 * se
print("Mean:", round(tb, 2))
print("Standard error:", round(se, 2))
print("Confidence interval:", round(thap, 2), "to", round(cao, 2))
print("Conclusion:", "different from 0" if thap > 0 or cao < 0 else "not enough to say it differs from 0")

sections.title: Four times the data, only twice as precise
sections.caption: Illustrative figures: the weekly standard deviation is yours to set. The standard error falls with the square root of the number of weeks, so going from 16 to 64 weeks only halves it. Sampling more densely within the same weeks does not change n, so it does not pull this line down.

lines: A number without a confidence interval is an opinion in make-up.
The next lesson turns this into a formal procedure: hypothesis testing.
